events.title: First Animal in Earth Orbit
events.blurb: A stray mixed-breed dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, a 508 kg spacecraft with no reentry capability. Laika survived liftoff and initial orbit but died from overheating within five to seven hours when a thermal regulation system failed — a fact withheld from the public for decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1957 — Sputnik 2. The Soviets announced Laika died painlessly after several days; the truth wasn't confirmed until 2002. The spacecraft had been built in under four weeks on Khrushchev's orders to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. Laika has since been honored with a monument in Moscow and a postage stamp in more than 70 countries.

events.title: First Soft Moon Landing
events.blurb: The Soviet Luna 9 spacecraft landed intact on the Ocean of Storms, becoming the first vehicle to achieve a controlled soft landing on another world and transmit photographs from the surface. Its four petal-shaped panels opened to right the lander and deploy an antenna, then it sent back a panoramic image sequence over three sessions totaling nine images.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1966 — Luna 9. British radio astronomers at Jodrell Bank intercepted the transmission and noticed it used the same format as a standard wire-photo machine. They borrowed a Müller facsimile unit from a news agency and published the images before the Soviets released them officially — to Moscow's considerable irritation.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Hubble Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Discovery deployed the Hubble Space Telescope into a 612 km orbit, positioning a 2.4-meter primary mirror above Earth's atmosphere to capture ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light without atmospheric distortion. The primary mirror was later found to have been ground 2.2 micrometers too flat — a spherical aberration correctable only by a servicing mission.
events.revealBlurb: April 24, 1990 — STS-31. The mirror flaw came from a testing lens installed backward by 1.3 mm. Three years later, astronauts installed corrective optics during the first Hubble servicing mission — essentially fitting the telescope with contact lenses. Hubble has since produced more than 1.5 million observations.

events.title: Columbia Reentry Breakup
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated over Texas and Louisiana during reentry, killing all seven crew members 16 minutes before its scheduled landing. A 1.2 kg piece of insulating foam had struck the leading edge of the left wing at liftoff 16 days earlier, breaching a reinforced carbon-carbon thermal protection panel and allowing superheated plasma to enter the wing structure during descent.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2003 — STS-107. Columbia was the oldest shuttle in the fleet, on its 28th mission. Debris was recovered across 2,000 km of Texas and Louisiana; some experiments in sealed canisters survived, including a container of worms (C. elegans) that lived through the breakup. It was the second shuttle lost in 113 flights.

events.title: Stockton-Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A 40-kilometre railway built to carry coal from the inland pits of County Durham to the shipping harbour at Stockton-on-Tees opened with a locomotive designed by a former colliery engineer pulling a 30-wagon train of coal, flour, and 600 passengers. It was the first public railway to use a steam locomotive for passenger service. Horse-drawn wagons continued to share the line for its first decades.
events.revealBlurb: September 27, 1825 — engineer George Stephenson, his locomotive "Locomotion No. 1." On the opening day Stephenson himself drove the engine, reaching a giddy top speed of 24 km/h. The railway ran until nationalization in 1948.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: First Moving Assembly Line
events.blurb: A Detroit automobile company introduced a moving chassis-assembly line at its Highland Park plant, cutting the time needed to assemble a car from 12 hours to 93 minutes. The innovation — borrowed in part from Chicago meatpacking "disassembly" lines — let the company slash prices and dramatically increase production. The line's relentless pace was hated by workers; the company had to double wages the following year to keep them on the job.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1913 — Ford Motor Company, Highland Park plant. The $5/day wage (equivalent to about $140/day today) followed on January 5, 1914. Workers' turnover at the plant dropped from 370 percent annually to near zero. The wage offer drew applicants by the thousands; police had to turn away crowds in a near-riot.

events.title: Korean War Begins
events.blurb: In the pre-dawn darkness, roughly 75,000 soldiers of a northern peninsular state poured south across the 38th parallel, overwhelming border defenses and driving south within days. The United Nations Security Council, with the Soviet representative boycotting, voted to intervene — the first shooting war between major powers since 1945.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1950 — Kim Il-sung's forces crossed the parallel. The USSR was boycotting the UN over China's representation, which is why the Soviet veto didn't stop intervention. MacArthur's Inchon landing three months later turned the war.

events.title: McCarthy Wheeling Speech
events.blurb: At a Lincoln Day dinner in West Virginia, a previously obscure U.S. senator brandished a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known communists working in the State Department. The charge, later revised repeatedly and never substantiated, launched a four-year domestic witch-hunt that would bear his name.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1950 — Joseph McCarthy, up for re-election, stumbled onto his signature issue. The "list" he waved kept changing: 205, then 57, then 81. No copy of the original was ever produced. It destroyed thousands of careers anyway.

events.title: Suez Crisis
events.blurb: Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt to seize the nationalized waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The military operation succeeded; the political one did not. Under combined U.S. and Soviet pressure, the invaders withdrew within two months. The affair is remembered as the moment Britain stopped being a great power.
events.revealBlurb: October 29 to November 7, 1956 — Eisenhower was furious he hadn't been consulted and threatened to sell US holdings of British sterling. British PM Anthony Eden resigned in disgrace three months later. Nasser emerged as the hero of the Arab world.

events.title: Berlin Wall Built
events.blurb: Overnight, East German soldiers and workers unrolled barbed wire along the jagged frontier between the two halves of a divided city, cutting off the escape route that some 3.5 million people had used to flee west over the previous twelve years. Within days the wire was replaced with concrete. Families woke to find themselves permanently separated from relatives one street away.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1961 — construction began at 2 AM on a Sunday. The wall eventually grew to 155 kilometres, with 302 watchtowers and a "death strip" of raked sand and trip-wires. At least 140 people died trying to cross it going west.

events.title: Moscow-Washington Hotline
events.blurb: Shaken by how close they had come to nuclear war the previous October, the United States and Soviet Union signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a direct teleprinter link between their capitals. Contrary to Hollywood, it was never a red telephone — it was a clunky, secure teletype system. The first test message read: "THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG."
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1963 — signed in Geneva. The line was first used in earnest in 1967 during the Arab-Israeli War. Today it's a secure email system; neither side actually picks up a red phone.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Birkenau Gas Chambers Operational
events.blurb: Four large purpose-built structures combining undressing rooms, sealed chambers, and industrial crematoria were completed and put into continuous operation at a camp in occupied Poland, creating a killing capacity of several thousand people per day and establishing the industrial infrastructure used to murder the majority of the Holocaust's victims.
events.revealBlurb: The four large crematoria-gas chamber complexes at Auschwitz-Birkenau came fully operational between March and June 1943. At peak operation in the summer of 1944, during the deportation of Hungarian Jews, they killed and cremated up to 10,000 people per day. The Sonderkommando — prisoner workers forced to operate the crematoria — later buried written testimony in the ash.

events.title: Yalta Conference
events.blurb: Three heads of government convened at a palatial Crimean resort to decide the political geography of the postwar world — agreeing on the division of a defeated nation into occupation zones, the formation of a new international peace organisation, and the borders of several countries whose populations had no vote in the matter.
events.revealBlurb: February 4–11, 1945. FDR was visibly ill — he would be dead in two months — and Soviet diplomats exploited his eagerness for a deal. Stalin's concessions on free elections in Eastern Europe proved worthless within two years. Churchill reportedly told his doctor: "I do not suppose that at any moment in history has the agony of the world been so great or widespread."

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Janet Jackson Super Bowl Halftime
events.blurb: An American pop singer, performing with Justin Timberlake at a Super Bowl halftime show, experienced a "wardrobe malfunction" — Timberlake pulled at her leather bustier at the end of their duet, exposing her right breast for 9/16ths of a second on live television. The incident produced an estimated $550,000 in regulatory fines, congressional hearings, and a lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court. It effectively launched YouTube (co-founder Jawed Karim said later that the desire to re-watch the moment inspired the site). Timberlake's career was barely touched; Jackson's was permanently diminished.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2004 — Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show in Houston. The word "wardrobe malfunction" entered the English language. A 2020 retrospective documentary drew new attention to how asymmetrically the American public had blamed Jackson.

events.title: Whitney Houston Dies
events.blurb: A 48-year-old American singer with one of the most powerful voices in pop music history was found unresponsive in a bathtub at a Beverly Hills hotel. The cause of death was accidental drowning complicated by heart disease and cocaine use. She had been scheduled to attend a Grammy Awards pre-party that evening. Her death came the night before the Grammys themselves, which had to be hastily rewritten to include a tribute. Seven years later her only daughter would die under similar circumstances.
events.revealBlurb: February 11, 2012 — Whitney Houston at the Beverly Hilton. Daughter Bobbi Kristina Brown, 22, was found unresponsive in a bathtub on January 31, 2015 and died six months later. Houston's "I Will Always Love You" had been the bestselling single by a woman in history until Adele surpassed it.

events.title: Harambe Killed
events.blurb: A 17-year-old western lowland gorilla at the Cincinnati Zoo was shot and killed by zoo staff after a 3-year-old boy climbed through a barrier and fell into the gorilla enclosure. The zoo explained that the gorilla had grabbed the child and dragged him through the water; tranquilizer darts would have taken too long. The killing triggered a wave of online outrage, internet memes, and several years' worth of "RIP Harambe" jokes that became a meta-joke of 2010s internet culture.
events.revealBlurb: May 28, 2016 — Harambe, Cincinnati Zoo. The child recovered fully. The zoo director Thane Maynard defended the decision as the only available option. The Harambe meme's peculiar staying power has been studied as a case of absurdist internet grief; election-poll write-in votes for Harambe persisted for years.

events.title: Stranger Things Premieres
events.blurb: A supernatural drama set in a small Indiana town in 1983 premiered on Netflix, combining Spielbergian child adventure, Stephen King atmospheric horror, and 80s-movie production design with a pitch-perfect synth-wave score. The 8-episode first season was Netflix's first genuine original-production cultural sensation and proved that the streaming service could create prestige-TV hits without a traditional network. The cast of unknown child actors became overnight celebrities.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2016 — Netflix; created by the Duffer Brothers. Cast included Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Noah Schnapp. The 2022 season 4 episode "Running Up That Hill" pushed Kate Bush's 1985 single to #1 in the UK, 37 years after its original release.

events.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events.blurb: American militia who had occupied two hills on a peninsula north of Boston overnight were assaulted by British regulars advancing uphill in three waves. The defenders — reportedly told "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" to conserve ammunition — inflicted heavy casualties on the first two waves before running out of powder and being driven from the ground. The British held the field but lost over 1,000 men; the American cause gained enormous moral prestige.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1775 — fought mostly on Breed's Hill; misnamed after the adjacent Bunker Hill. British commander: General Thomas Gage. American commander killed in the retreat: General Joseph Warren. Within days, Congress appointed George Washington commander-in-chief.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Franco-American Alliance
events.blurb: A French-American treaty signed in Paris transformed the American rebellion into a global war. France, which had been secretly funneling weapons and volunteers to the rebels through front companies, formally recognized American independence, committed its navy to the war, and in return secured commercial terms with the new republic. Spain joined the next year, the Netherlands the year after, and Britain soon found herself fighting Europe's great powers on multiple oceans.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1778 — Treaty of Alliance, Paris. Benjamin Franklin, the Americans' chief diplomat, had worked the French court for two years in a coonskin cap that French aristocrats found exotically charming. France's participation in the war contributed significantly to its own fiscal collapse a decade later.

events.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.blurb: The French National Constituent Assembly, meeting in a recently converted royal indoor tennis court, adopted a 17-article statement of universal rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of speech and religion. It did not grant women the vote or abolish slavery; revolutionaries would debate those extensions for years. It was still the most sweeping such declaration any European state had ever adopted.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1789 — a central drafter was the Marquis de Lafayette, the American Revolution veteran. The declaration was explicitly modeled on the U.S. Declaration of Independence; in fact, Jefferson, then in Paris as American minister, advised on its drafting. It remains part of France's constitutional law.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin Released
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet director released a 75-minute silent film dramatizing a 1905 mutiny on a Russian imperial battleship. Its centerpiece, a massacre sequence on a flight of stone stairs in the Black Sea port city of Odessa, introduced a style of rapid associative editing that reshaped 20th-century cinema. A baby's pram bounces downward through the gunfire in a shot that has been quoted by dozens of later filmmakers.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1925 — Sergei Eisenstein. The Odessa Steps massacre is fictional; no such event occurred in 1905. The pram shot has been homaged in The Untouchables, Brazil, and The Simpsons. Joseph Goebbels reportedly called the film "a marvelous film without equal."

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Parasite Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A 50-year-old South Korean director's satirical thriller about a poor family insinuating itself into a wealthy family's household became the first non-English-language film to win the top prize at a major U.S. film awards ceremony. It also took Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, and Best International Feature — a quadruple sweep by a "foreign" film that industry observers had long thought impossible. The director thanked Martin Scorsese in one of his acceptance speeches.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 2020 — Bong Joon-ho's "Parasite" at the 92nd Academy Awards. The film's Korean-language narrative beat Sam Mendes's "1917" and Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood." It was also the first Palme d'Or winner to win Best Picture in 65 years.

events.title: Euclid's Elements Written
events.blurb: A 13-book mathematical treatise organised geometry, number theory, and proportion into a rigorous deductive system built from five simple axioms and five postulates, from which hundreds of theorems were derived by logical proof alone. The work became the model for mathematical reasoning for more than two thousand years and remained a standard university textbook in parts of Europe into the twentieth century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 300 BCE — almost nothing is known about Euclid himself; even his birthdate is unknown. The Elements is the second most-printed book in history after the Bible. One of its five postulates — the parallel postulate — resisted proof for two thousand years; mathematicians who tried to derive it instead invented non-Euclidean geometry.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Radioactivity Discovered
events.blurb: A French physicist studying uranium salts placed a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer alongside a uranium sample during several cloudy days, expecting to run a sunlight experiment later. When he developed the plate anyway, he found a sharp image — proving the uranium was spontaneously emitting invisible radiation with no external energy source, a phenomenon no existing theory could explain.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1896 — Henri Becquerel announced to the Academy of Sciences that the image was "very distinct." The discovery was accidental: bad weather cancelled his planned sunlight experiment. He initially thought it was a variant of X-rays; it took the Curies to show radioactivity was a property of the atom itself.

events.title: Quantum Theory Proposed
events.blurb: To solve an embarrassing mathematical failure in explaining how hot objects radiate energy, a German physicist proposed a radical hypothesis: that energy is not emitted in a continuous stream but in discrete, indivisible packets whose size is proportional to frequency. He called these packets "quanta" and introduced a new constant of nature — later named Planck's constant — relating energy to frequency.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1900 — Max Planck later admitted he introduced the quantum as a mathematical trick he expected to discard once he found a better formula. He told his son he had just made "a discovery as important as Newton's." It took Einstein's 1905 photoelectric paper to convince physicists that quanta were real.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: Mozart's Requiem Unfinished
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Austrian composer who had been commissioned by a mysterious stranger six months earlier to compose a requiem Mass for an anonymous client died in his Vienna apartment with the work unfinished. Much of the "Dies irae" and "Lacrimosa" had been sketched only. His widow, in desperate financial circumstances, had a student complete the work to secure the remaining half of the commission fee.
events.revealBlurb: December 5, 1791 — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35. The mysterious stranger was Count Walsegg, who meant to pass the work off as his own for his late wife. Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it; his contributions have been debated ever since.

events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Red Cross Founded
events.blurb: A committee of five Swiss citizens, led by a Geneva businessman who had witnessed the aftermath of a bloody Italian battle four years earlier and published a book about the unimaginable suffering of wounded soldiers left untreated on the field, established an international humanitarian organization to provide medical care to the wounded in war. Their emblem — a red cross on a white field, the Swiss flag inverted — was chosen as a neutral symbol protecting aid workers.
events.revealBlurb: February 17, 1863 — International Committee of the Red Cross, founded by Henry Dunant and four others in Geneva. Dunant won the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 despite being nearly penniless. The Muslim world adopted the Red Crescent in 1876; Israel uses a Red Crystal, adopted 2005.

events.title: Röntgen Discovers X-Rays
events.blurb: A 50-year-old German physicist, working with a cathode-ray tube covered in black cardboard, noticed that a paper screen coated in barium platinocyanide glowed even when placed some distance away. He realized the tube was emitting an invisible, unknown type of radiation. Further experiments showed the rays penetrated paper, wood, aluminum, and even human flesh — but not bone. He published an image of his wife's hand, showing her skeleton and wedding ring.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen at the University of Würzburg. He called the phenomenon "X" rays because he didn't know what they were. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The image of his wife's hand, published in early 1896, is arguably the first diagnostic X-ray.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Human Genome Draft Published
events.blurb: Two groups — the international Human Genome Project consortium and the private company Celera Genomics, which had entered the race late with a competing methodology — simultaneously published their draft sequences of the 3 billion base pairs of the human genome in the journals Nature and Science. The entries were the culmination of 11 years of work and a vast investment of computing and laboratory resources. Humans had roughly 21,000 genes — far fewer than most biologists had predicted.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 2001 — publications in Nature (consortium) and Science (Celera). The "finished" version of the sequence arrived in 2003. Sequencing a human genome now costs about $200 (down from $2.7 billion) and takes a day.

events.title: Bayeux Tapestry Completed
events.blurb: An embroidered strip of linen 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, worked in coloured wool yarns, depicts in 58 scenes the Norman conquest of a cross-Channel kingdom — the diplomatic prelude, the invasion fleet, a victorious battle, and the death of a king by arrow. It includes 623 human figures, 202 horses, 55 dogs, and a Latin commentary running across the top.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1077 — commissioned either by Bishop Odo of Bayeux or Queen Matilda. Despite its name, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. It survived the French Revolution only because a local lawyer hid it when a crowd tried to use it to cover an ammunition wagon.

events.title: The Last Supper Completed
events.blurb: An Italian polymath completed a 9-metre-wide mural in the refectory of a Dominican convent in a northern Italian city, depicting Christ announcing his betrayal and the instant of shocked reaction on the faces of his twelve disciples. The artist had worked on it for three years, painting in oil on a dry wall rather than true fresco — a choice that made the picture deteriorate visibly within his own lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: 1498 — Leonardo da Vinci in Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. His experimental technique began flaking within 20 years. The painting has been restored many times, most recently between 1978 and 1999. Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed the refectory roof but the wall survived.

events.title: Rembrandt's Night Watch
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter completed a 3.6 by 4.4 metre group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company, commissioned by 18 civic-guard officers each paying 100 guilders for his place. Unlike the static lineup portraits typical of the genre, the painter depicted the company in motion, emerging from a shadowed arch with a drum rolling and a musket firing. The title "Night Watch" is a misnomer added by 19th-century curators; varnish had darkened a daytime scene.
events.revealBlurb: 1642 — Rembrandt van Rijn. Now in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum. It was trimmed on all sides in 1715 to fit between two doorways, losing two figures. A recent 8K restoration reconstructed the missing pieces using AI.

events.title: First Impressionist Exhibition
events.blurb: Thirty painters whose work had been repeatedly rejected by the official French Salon rented the studio of a photographer on a Paris boulevard and held their own group show. A review in a satirical magazine mocked one of the paintings — "Impression, Sunrise" — and gave the movement the name it would keep. The show attracted 3,500 visitors, which was dismal; mockery outweighed admiration; most of the painters struggled financially for another decade.
events.revealBlurb: April 15 to May 15, 1874 — 35 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris. Participants included Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Cézanne, Berthe Morisot, and Sisley. The critic who coined the term, Louis Leroy, titled his review "Exhibition of the Impressionists" sarcastically; the painters adopted it.

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: NAACP Founded
events.blurb: A biracial group of activists, scholars, and newspaper editors met at a New York conference on the centennial of Abraham Lincoln's birth to establish an organization dedicated to fighting racial discrimination through legal action and public advocacy. W.E.B. Du Bois, the Harvard-trained sociologist, edited its magazine The Crisis; its lawyers would eventually argue Brown v. Board of Education.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1909 — National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It was founded partly in response to the Springfield, Illinois race riot the year before. Du Bois served as editor of The Crisis for 24 years.

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964 Signed
events.blurb: President Lyndon Johnson signed the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations — ending the legal architecture of Jim Crow segregation. The bill passed after the longest Senate filibuster in history: 57 days.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1964 — The White House. Johnson reportedly told an aide after signing the bill, "We have lost the South for a generation" — a reference to the political realignment he expected. Johnson signed the bill with 75 ceremonial pens, handing them to civil rights leaders and the bill's sponsors.

events.title: Freedom Summer Murders
events.blurb: Three voter-registration volunteers — two Jewish New Yorkers and a local Black civil rights worker — disappeared after being arrested for an alleged traffic violation, released at night, and abducted by Klansmen near a Mississippi town. Their bodies were found 44 days later, bulldozed into an earthen dam. A massive FBI manhunt — the first major civil rights intervention by the Bureau — cracked the case.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1964 — Philadelphia, Mississippi. James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner. The state refused to prosecute; federal civil-rights conspiracy charges netted seven convictions. The ringleader, Edgar Ray Killen, was finally convicted of manslaughter in 2005 at age 80.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Facebook Buys WhatsApp
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley social-networking giant announced an agreement to acquire a five-year-old messaging app with 450 million users for $19 billion in cash and stock — the largest venture-backed acquisition in tech history. The app had 55 employees; one of its two founders had been rejected when he applied for a job at Facebook eight years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 2014 — Facebook buys WhatsApp; co-founders Jan Koum and Brian Acton. The service had been run on the principle of no ads, no gimmicks; Acton later left Facebook over disagreements about monetization and funded the rival Signal.

events.title: Pokémon Go Released
events.blurb: A free mobile game combining augmented reality with a beloved monster-catching franchise launched initially in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Within a week, 21 million daily active users were wandering streets and parks staring at their phones, discovering virtual creatures superimposed on physical landmarks. It became the fastest mobile game to reach $500 million in revenue and, more strikingly, got millions of sedentary users to walk outside.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Niantic Inc. Within weeks, fatal accidents, trespassing incidents, and a small bump in physical activity had all been documented. The Pokémon Go wedding, held in New York's Central Park, was among the odder cultural moments of mid-2016.

events.title: Ashoka Conquers Kalinga
events.blurb: A Mauryan emperor's army conquered a fiercely resistant coastal kingdom after a war that, by the emperor's own inscriptions, killed 100,000 people and displaced 150,000 more. Revolted by the carnage he had ordered, the emperor publicly renounced war, embraced a philosophy of non-violence, and had pillars erected across his realm inscribed with edicts of compassion — the earliest dateable Indian texts we can read today.
events.revealBlurb: c. 261 BCE — Ashoka the Great, Maurya dynasty. The lion capital from his pillar at Sarnath — four lions standing back to back — is now India's national emblem.

events.title: Rajaraja Chola I Consecrates the Brihadeeswarar Temple
events.blurb: The most powerful ruler of the Chola dynasty, having conquered Sri Lanka, the Maldives, and swaths of Southeast Asia, consecrated a temple to Shiva in his capital Thanjavur. The vimanam — its central tower — rose 66 metres from a foundation that required no scaffolding from the outside: the stone was hauled up a 6-kilometre ramp. The capstone alone, carved from a single block of granite, weighs 80 tonnes.
events.revealBlurb: 1010 CE — Rajaraja Chola I, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Brihadeeswarar Temple was built in just seven years, has stood for over a thousand, and its tower casts no shadow at noon on a midsummer day. Engineers still aren't entirely sure how they pulled that off.

events.title: Akbar Secures the Mughal Throne
events.blurb: A 13-year-old Mughal prince was crowned emperor at Kalanaur, Punjab, moments after his father fell down a library staircase in Delhi. His regent Bairam Khan immediately faced a formidable rival — the Hindu general Hemu, who had taken Delhi with 30,000 cavalry and 1,500 war elephants. At the second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was felled by a stray arrow mid-battle, his army collapsed, and the boy king's empire was saved.
events.revealBlurb: February 1556 CE — Akbar the Great. The same king who would later abolish the jizya tax, marry Rajput princesses, invent a syncretic religion, and reportedly have three thousand women in his harem started his reign as a frightened teenager hiding behind his general.

events.title: Aurangzeb Imprisons His Father Shah Jahan
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor fell ill, setting off a fratricidal war among his four sons. The third son, Aurangzeb, outmaneuvered his brothers militarily and politically — defeating one at the Battle of Samugarh, executing another, driving the third into exile — then declared his father too weak to rule and locked him in the Agra Fort. Shah Jahan remained imprisoned there for eight years until his death, attended only by his devoted daughter Jahanara.
events.revealBlurb: July 1658 CE — Aurangzeb seizes the Mughal throne. Shah Jahan's prison quarters in Agra Fort had a view of the Taj Mahal across the river, built for his late wife. Contemporary sources say Jahanara placed a mirror so he could see it from his sickbed.

events.title: The Marathas Are Defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Maratha army of 45,000 soldiers and 200,000 camp followers — including families who had brought their children on what they expected to be a triumphant northern campaign — faced an Afghan force under the Durrani king. After an eight-month standoff that left the Marathas starving, they were crushed in a single morning. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops died in the battle; up to 40,000 prisoners were massacred the following day.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 1761 — Ahmad Shah Durrani vs. Sadashivrao Bhau, Panipat. Fought on the same plain as two earlier world-changing battles. The Maratha defeat ended Hindu imperial ambitions and opened India to British expansion. It is said that barely a family in the Deccan was not in mourning afterward.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Fall of Singapore
events.blurb: An island fortress considered impregnable from the sea fell in one week when attackers crossed a narrow strait at its land-facing back and advanced down a peninsula faster than anyone had thought possible. The surrender of 80,000 troops in a single capitulation stands as the largest in the history of the British Army.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1942. General Percival surrendered at 6:20 PM. Churchill called it "the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history." The great naval guns of Singapore pointed seaward and many lacked armour-piercing shells anyway — the attack had come from the wrong direction entirely.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: Allied Invasion of Sicily
events.blurb: The largest amphibious operation to that point in military history put 160,000 troops, 3,000 ships, and 4,000 aircraft onto a Mediterranean island in a single night and day — opening the Allied campaign on the European continent itself and within three weeks causing the arrest and removal of a dictator who had held power for two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 9–10, 1943 — Operation Husky. Benito Mussolini was deposed by his own Fascist Grand Council on July 25, just two weeks after the landings. An elaborate Allied deception operation, "Operation Mincemeat," had planted false documents on a corpse washed ashore in Spain suggesting the real target was Greece — and the Germans believed it.

events.title: Death of Hitler
events.blurb: The dictator who had triggered the continent's most destructive conflict, directed the murder of millions, and sworn never to be taken alive shot himself in a subterranean command centre beneath a capital city now surrounded by enemy armies, having married his companion the previous day and designated a naval admiral as his successor.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1945 — Hitler shot himself at approximately 3:30 PM in the Führerbunker; Eva Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried to the garden and burned. By explicit prior order, no intact corpse was to fall into enemy hands. Soviet forces found the remains eight days after the surrender; Stalin kept the truth of their forensic identification secret for decades.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: Pyaasa Released
events.blurb: A poet who the city believes to be dead wanders through venal publishers and indifferent relatives in a film Guru Dutt both directed and starred in, constructing one of Indian cinema's most sustained indictments of commercialised culture through Sahir Ludhianvi's Urdu verse set to S.D. Burman's music. Time magazine later placed it among the 100 greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1957 — Guru Dutt's masterwork. The film was semi-autobiographical; Dutt was increasingly alienated from the Bombay film industry's values, an estrangement he did not survive — he died in 1964, aged 39. The song "Jaane Woh Kaise Log The" remains among the most covered in Hindi film music.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: Slumdog Millionaire Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A British-directed film set entirely in Mumbai — shot partly in the Dharavi slum with non-professional child actors, partly in the chaos of the city's streets — swept eight Oscars including Best Picture at the 81st Academy Awards, making it the first film primarily set and cast in India to win the top prize. Its pavement-to-riches structure was lifted directly from Bollywood's own playbook.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 2009. Directed by Danny Boyle. A.R. Rahman won Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Jai Ho" — his first Oscars, received in the same night. The child actors from the film were discovered to be living in poverty after production wrapped, triggering international headlines.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Completed
events.blurb: A German goldsmith completed printing a 1,286-page Latin Bible using a press with movable metal type, producing an estimated 180 copies at a rate no scribe could approach. Each sheet required individually set letter blocks cast in an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — making it the first book in Europe produced by mechanical movable type.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Magellan Sets Sail
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Portuguese-born captain, working for the Spanish crown because his own king had rejected his project, left a Sevillian port with five small ships and 270 men on a westward voyage to the spice-rich islands of Southeast Asia. He was convinced a sea passage through the Americas existed. He would find it — and a strait at the continent's southern tip is now named after him — but he would never see its other end.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1519 — Ferdinand Magellan. He was killed on the Philippine island of Mactan on April 27, 1521 by troops of the local chief Lapu-Lapu. One of his five ships completed the first circumnavigation — returning with 18 survivors and a load of cloves that covered the entire expedition's costs.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.blurb: The first Bourbon king of France, a former Protestant who had converted to Catholicism to secure his crown ("Paris is worth a Mass"), issued an edict guaranteeing Protestant Huguenots freedom of worship in specific towns, civil equality, and the right to maintain their own fortified places. The compromise ended 36 years of Wars of Religion and was the most expansive grant of religious toleration any European state had yet made. His grandson would revoke it 87 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1598 — Henry IV of France. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, triggering a Protestant exodus of perhaps 400,000 skilled workers. Henry IV himself was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.title: ENIAC Unveiled
events.blurb: Engineers at an American university publicly demonstrated an 27-tonne general-purpose electronic computer, filling a 30 by 15 metre room with 17,468 vacuum tubes, 10,000 capacitors, and 6,000 switches. The machine calculated artillery-shell trajectories 2,400 times faster than a human with an adding machine. Programming it required physically rewiring hundreds of cables; the programmers — all women — had to crawl inside to swap plugs.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1946 — University of Pennsylvania. Designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman. They were not invited to the unveiling dinner; their faces were cropped out of celebratory photos for decades.

events.title: Transistor Invented
events.blurb: Three physicists at an American industrial research laboratory demonstrated a working point-contact transistor — a tiny semiconductor device made from germanium that could amplify electrical signals without the vacuum tubes, heat, and bulk then required. Within a decade the invention had reshaped electronics; within five decades, billions of its descendants would fit on a single silicon chip smaller than a fingernail.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1947 — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel. Shockley's later semiconductor company, though commercially a failure, seeded Silicon Valley through the departure of its "Traitorous Eight" founders of Fairchild Semiconductor.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Watson Wins Jeopardy
events.blurb: An IBM supercomputer named after the company's founder competed over three nights of a televised American trivia game show against the two greatest human champions the show had ever produced — and won by a wide margin. The machine had been fed a corpus of Wikipedia, encyclopedias, and dictionaries; it processed buzzer-triggered natural-language clues with a complex pipeline of heuristics and statistical models. It was not a single breakthrough; it was an engineering triumph.
events.revealBlurb: February 14-16, 2011 — Watson vs. Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. Jennings' final written answer on night three: "I, for one, welcome our new computer overlords." IBM spent heavily trying to commercialize Watson for healthcare and business; most of those products have since been divested or discontinued.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: The Feminine Mystique Published
events.blurb: A former labour journalist who had been writing articles for women's magazines published a 410-page book analyzing what she called "the problem that has no name" — the stifling dissatisfaction of educated suburban housewives. It sold three million copies within three years and became the foundational text of a resurgent American feminist movement that would transform employment law, education policy, and reproductive rights.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 1963 — Betty Friedan. The book drew on her research into a Smith College alumni survey. Friedan went on to co-found the National Organization for Women in 1966 and help lead the 1970 Women's Strike for Equality.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Junko Tabei Summits Everest
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Japanese climber, buried by an avalanche at 6,300 metres twelve days earlier and unconscious for six minutes until fellow climbers dug her out, reached the summit of the world's highest mountain with her Sherpa guide. She was the first woman to stand on top of it. She had self-funded the expedition with 15 others by teaching piano and editing a scientific journal; she sewed her own gear from scrap material.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1975 — Junko Tabei. She went on to climb the highest mountain on every continent by 1992, the first woman to do so. She died of cancer in 2016, aged 77, having continued climbing almost to the end.

events.title: Kamala Harris Becomes VP
events.blurb: A 56-year-old U.S. senator from California, whose mother had immigrated from India and father from Jamaica, was sworn in on the steps of the U.S. Capitol as the nation's 49th vice president, the first woman, first African-American, and first Asian-American to hold the office. She was sworn in by the first Latina Supreme Court justice, on two bibles: one from Justice Thurgood Marshall's widow and one from a close family friend.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 2021 — sworn in by Justice Sonia Sotomayor. The inauguration, held two weeks after the January 6 Capitol attack, proceeded behind 25,000 National Guard troops. Harris later became the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee after Joe Biden withdrew.

events.title: Wilt Chamberlain's 100-Point Game
events.blurb: A 25-year-old 7-foot-1 Philadelphia Warriors center scored 100 points in a regular-season NBA game — 36 field goals, 28 free throws, a record that has never been approached since. The game, played at a neutral-site arena in a central Pennsylvania city, drew only 4,124 spectators; no television footage survives, and only one photograph of the 100-point moment exists. The center himself had scored 50 on a different occasion just weeks earlier; a 100-point game almost seemed inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1962 — Wilt Chamberlain, Philadelphia vs. New York Knicks at Hershey, PA. Final score: Warriors 169, Knicks 147. The iconic photo shows Chamberlain holding a piece of paper reading "100" in the locker room. His career scoring average of 30.1 points per game remains second only to Michael Jordan.

events.title: Cassius Clay Shocks Liston
events.blurb: A 22-year-old loud-talking boxer from Louisville, a 7-1 underdog against the seemingly invincible heavyweight champion, danced around his opponent for six rounds, cut him under the eye in the third, and won the world title when the champion refused to answer the bell for the seventh round. He skipped around the ring shouting "I am the greatest!" to reporters who had mostly written him off as doomed. He would change his name to one the world would remember the next morning.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1964 — Cassius Clay defeated Sonny Liston in Miami Beach. Clay announced his new name, Muhammad Ali, two days later, having joined the Nation of Islam. He would win 56 of his 61 professional bouts and lose his prime years to a Vietnam War draft controversy.

events.title: The Rumble in the Jungle
events.blurb: A 32-year-old heavyweight boxing challenger, widely predicted to lose to the younger and vastly more powerful champion, leaned back against the ropes for seven rounds and absorbed punishing body blows — a tactic he later nicknamed "rope-a-dope." In the 8th, when the champion visibly tired, the challenger delivered a flurry of punches that knocked him out. The fight was held in an African capital as part of a pioneering pan-African promotion.
events.revealBlurb: October 30, 1974 — Muhammad Ali KO'd George Foreman at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo). Promoter Don King organized it. The event was immortalized in the 1996 documentary "When We Were Kings."

events.title: Miracle on Ice
events.blurb: A U.S. college-aged men's hockey team, facing a Soviet Union team that had won five of the previous six Olympic gold medals and was widely considered the best in the world, won 4-3 at a Lake Placid Winter Olympics with a third-period game-winning goal by the team's captain. The victory, during a tense period of Cold War tensions and a national recession, was broadcast on delayed tape; the announcer's closing cry — "Do you believe in miracles? YES!" — became one of the most-replayed lines in American sports.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1980 — US vs USSR at the Lake Placid Olympics. Coach: Herb Brooks. The US went on to win the gold medal by beating Finland two days later. The captain was Mike Eruzione. Al Michaels was the ABC announcer.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: Nixon Visits China
events.blurb: A U.S. president whose entire career had been built on anti-communist credentials stepped off Air Force One in the Chinese capital to shake hands with the leader of a nation Washington had refused to recognize for 23 years. The week-long visit, carefully choreographed after two years of secret diplomacy, upended the bipolar world order and drove a wedge between the two great communist powers.
events.revealBlurb: February 21-28, 1972 — Richard Nixon meets Mao Zedong. Henry Kissinger had flown secretly to Beijing via Pakistan the previous summer to arrange it. The phrase "Nixon goes to China" has since become shorthand for a politician doing something only his base could forgive.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.blurb: A Persian king who had already conquered Media, Lydia, and the Ionian cities entered the ancient city of Babylon without a fight, claiming to have been welcomed by its priests as the rightful king of the gods. His subsequent proclamation — known from a surviving cuneiform cylinder — repatriated exiled populations, restored local temples, and is sometimes described as the oldest surviving charter of human rights. The Persian Achaemenid Empire he founded became the largest the world had yet seen.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 539 BCE — Cyrus II. The Cyrus Cylinder is now in the British Museum. The Hebrew Bible credits Cyrus with allowing the Judean exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple; he is the only non-Jewish figure called "messiah" in the Hebrew scriptures.

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
