events.blurb: A force of 300 Spartan hoplites with their personal attendants, reinforced by perhaps 7,000 other Greek allies, held a narrow coastal pass for three days against a vastly larger Persian army. On the third day, betrayed by a local goatherd who revealed a mountain path, the Persians flanked the defenders. The Spartan king dismissed most of his allies and stayed with his three hundred to die. The sacrifice bought time for the evacuation of Athens and the Greek fleet's preparation.
events.revealBlurb: August 480 BCE — King Leonidas of Sparta vs. Xerxes I. Persian force size is debated; Herodotus' claim of millions is obviously inflated. Modern estimates suggest 70,000 to 300,000. "Molon labe" — "come and take them" — is Leonidas' reported reply to a demand that the Greeks surrender their arms.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Han Dynasty Founded
events.blurb: A former peasant who had risen through the collapsing Qin military to become a rebel general defeated his principal rival in a civil war and declared himself emperor, founding a dynasty that would rule China for four centuries. The Han synthesized Confucian political theory with Qin administrative machinery, ran the Silk Road trade with the West, invented paper, cast iron plowshares, and effectively defined the imperial Chinese civilization that would persist until 1911. The ethnic majority of modern China still calls itself "Han."
events.revealBlurb: 202 BCE — Liu Bang, posthumously Emperor Gaozu. He defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia. The Han dynasty is conventionally divided into the Western Han (202 BCE - 9 CE) and Eastern Han (25 CE - 220 CE), with a brief Wang Mang interregnum between.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Flag Raising on Iwo Jima
events.blurb: A photograph taken on a volcanic island's highest point captured six men raising a large flag over rubble and smoke, becoming one of the most reproduced images in history — and the model for a national memorial — though the battle it symbolised had barely begun and would last another five weeks at a cost exceeding 26,000 American casualties.
events.revealBlurb: February 23, 1945 — Joe Rosenthal's photograph was actually of the second flag raised that day; a smaller flag had gone up hours earlier. Three of the six men in the photograph were killed before the island was secured. Admiral Chester Nimitz observed: "Among the Americans who served on Iwo Jima, uncommon valor was a common virtue."

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Nagasaki
events.blurb: A second atomic strike, delivered three days after the first, detonated with the force of 22,000 tons of TNT over a city's industrial valley — but cloud cover over the primary target had forced the bomber to divert to its secondary, sparing one city and condemning another, while a city 160 kilometres away had been removed from the target list weeks earlier at the personal request of the American Secretary of War.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1945 — the B-29 Bockscar dropped "Fat Man" at 11:02 AM. Kokura, the original target, was obscured by clouds; pilot Sweeney diverted to Nagasaki. An estimated 40,000 died instantly; 80,000 total by year's end. Secretary of War Stimson had personally removed Kyoto from the target list because he had visited it on his honeymoon and loved it.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Spanish-American War Declaration
events.blurb: The United States declared war on Spain following the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor and years of lurid coverage of Spanish atrocities in Cuba by the American yellow press. The 114-day conflict ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and announced the United States as a Pacific and Caribbean imperial power.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1898 — Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to lead the volunteer Rough Riders cavalry regiment, charging up San Juan Hill — a battle that took one afternoon and made him president. Secretary of State John Hay called it "a splendid little war."

events.title: Atomic Bomb Dropped on Hiroshima
events.blurb: At 8:15 that morning, a B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay released a uranium bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" over the Japanese city of Hiroshima, which detonated at 1,968 feet above the city center with a force equivalent to approximately 15,000 tons of TNT. Estimates of deaths in the four months following the explosion range from 90,000 to 166,000; roughly two-thirds of the city's buildings were destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — Hiroshima, Japan. "Little Boy" was the first nuclear weapon ever used in warfare, but it had never been fully tested — scientists were confident enough in the gun-type design. Japan did not surrender after Hiroshima; it took a second bomb (Nagasaki, August 9) to produce the surrender announcement.

events.title: Nixon Resigns the Presidency
events.blurb: That evening, Richard Nixon became the first and only U.S. president to resign from office, delivering a nationally televised address from the Oval Office in which he announced his departure would take effect at noon the following day. The resignation came after the release of the "smoking gun" tape proved Nixon had personally directed the Watergate cover-up six days after the break-in, making his impeachment and Senate conviction certain.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1974 — The Oval Office. Nixon's approval rating the week of his resignation was 24%. Gerald Ford pardoned him one month later, saying "our long national nightmare is over" — a pardon that likely cost Ford the 1976 election. Nixon is the only president ever to resign.

events.title: New Coke Launched
events.blurb: A 99-year-old American beverage company launched a reformulated version of its flagship cola, sweeter and smoother, aimed at winning back market share from Pepsi in a rivalry called the Cola Wars. Blind taste tests had shown a preference for the new recipe; actual consumer response, once they knew what they were drinking, was widespread rage. Letters of protest poured into Atlanta; soda fountains advertised the return of the original. 79 days later, the company announced the comeback of "Coca-Cola Classic."
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 1985 — Coca-Cola. The original formula returned as "Coca-Cola Classic" on July 11, 1985. New Coke eventually became "Coke II" in 1992 and was quietly discontinued in 2002. The whole episode is now a business-school case study in consumer-brand attachment.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Verdict
events.blurb: A Los Angeles Superior Court jury, deliberating for only four hours after eleven months of testimony, found a former NFL running back and actor not guilty of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend. The verdict, announced at 10 AM Pacific time, was watched by an estimated 100 million Americans. National productivity visibly dropped during the broadcast. The decision split along racial lines: most white Americans believed him guilty; most Black Americans were skeptical of the Los Angeles police who had arrested him.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1995 — O.J. Simpson acquitted. Defense lawyers Johnnie Cochran ("If it doesn't fit, you must acquit") and Robert Shapiro. Simpson was later found liable for the deaths in a 1997 civil trial and ordered to pay $33.5 million. He died of cancer in April 2024 at 76.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: The Tale of Genji
events.blurb: A Japanese noblewoman serving at the imperial court of a Heian-era empress completed a 54-chapter prose narrative following the life, loves, and political career of a fictional son of an emperor. Full of psychological interiority, metaphorical poetry, and a sophisticated unreliable narrator, it is widely regarded as the world's first modern novel. It was written over more than a decade and circulated in manuscript among the court.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1010 CE — Murasaki Shikibu. The earliest surviving complete manuscript dates from the 13th century. It has been translated into English several times; Arthur Waley's 1925-33 version introduced it to the West, but recent translations are preferred for accuracy.

events.title: The Communist Manifesto
events.blurb: A 29-year-old German-born philosopher-journalist and his 27-year-old industrialist-heir collaborator published a 23-page political pamphlet commissioned by a small London-based workers' organization. Its opening sentence — about a spectre haunting Europe — and its closing rallying cry became arguably the most politically consequential prose of the 19th century. Within three weeks, revolutions were breaking out across the continent.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1848 — Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. The League of the Just commissioned it. The 1848 revolutions failed; the Manifesto didn't become widely read until the 1872 edition with a new preface. By the 20th century it had shaped the political systems of a third of humanity.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Space Invaders Hits Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: An alien formation that descended one row lower every time a column was destroyed — a quirk of the hardware clock — accidentally created the defining tension mechanic of arcade games. The game was so popular in Japan that bars converted into dedicated parlours.
events.revealBlurb: July 1978 — Taito released Space Invaders in Japan. The Atari 2600 home port in 1980 quadrupled console sales that year. The "yen coin shortage" is an urban legend — numismatists have found no evidence in mint records.

events.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Released for Sega Genesis
events.blurb: Sega needed a mascot to fight Mario. The result was a blue hedgehog who could run faster than the screen could scroll, built around a physics engine that turned speed itself into the core gameplay mechanic. It shipped bundled with the Genesis in North America, helped Sega capture 65 percent of the console market.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1991 — Sonic the Hedgehog launched in North America for the Sega Genesis. Sega's North American market share climbed from 15% to 65% during the game's first year. The Sonic franchise has since sold over 1.5 billion games.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Murder of Thomas Becket
events.blurb: Four knights, prompted by an angry outburst from their king over the head of the English church, rode to a cathedral in southern England and hacked the archbishop to death in his own nave after he refused to reconsider his excommunications of clergy who had sided with the king. The murder scandalized Christendom; pilgrimages to the martyr's tomb began within weeks and continued for 368 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 29, 1170 — Canterbury Cathedral, Thomas Becket killed by four knights of Henry II. The king's supposed outburst — "Who will rid me of this turbulent priest?" — may be apocryphal. Becket was canonized within three years; T.S. Eliot turned the story into "Murder in the Cathedral."

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.
